en: Making your road smooth,
May my father Shay, Zhol-Baabedin,
Protect you, my son!
May the hostile foe who confronts you
Find no fortune.
May mountains of black stone rise
Across your enemy’s road.
May your name spread throughout the world,
And may your lionheartedness be known, my son!
May no chill misfortune overtake you,
And may no rival defeat you.
Split the black hair with perfect judgment;
Be just toward my people!
May the people never turn against you!
My foals Kuyaly and Seytek,
If your hearts are wicked,
Your faults will bring forth evil.
Be fruit for the nation;
Heed the words I have spoken—
They will be wisdom for you.
If you become khan and maintain a court,
If you become a saintly soul,
If your fortune is complete,
May your name be heard by all who behold you;
Be a lion who shakes the world!
You, Seytek, be the gray-maned champion!
Your first forefather was a khan,
A wealthy man with teeming herds;
Every enemy he fought was laid low.
From among all souls came every hero,
The forty sons, all forty lions,
Who journeyed to Talas
And met the one who inherited the legacy,
Our forefather, the hero Manas.
He mastered the fattening of horses,
And though one man, he was worth forty.
Walking alone, he slew a thousand;
Take after your father and become a lion!
Become the leader of all the people,
My son Seytek.
Learn to join what has been severed;
Go forth and gather the scattered nation.
The ignorant who refuses to learn,
The one who will not heed spoken counsel,
The one who will not go where he is led—
Though he may be a close kinsman,
The scoundrel who knows no propriety,
The brute who understands no words—
In the end, do not hold him dear!
The one who knows nothing himself,
Who will not heed those who know,
Who pays regard to no one,
The fool duller than a camel—
Call him neither kinsman nor soul.
Do not say of the brute who knows no propriety,
‘He is one of our supporters,’
My son, or the people will speak of it!
Without a lion there is no hero;
Without heroes there is no war;
Without a mound there is no land;
Without eccentrics there is no people.
My son, without justice there is no khan;
Among the vast people no soul
Grows white-haired without a visitation from Khidr.
The common folk in your hands—
Value them like a moonlit lake.
In their depths, preserved from Kyrgyz Manas,
Lies the legacy of the treasury and wealth:
Slaughter and consume them, and they last one day;
Beat and drive them off, and they last one day;
Weigh their worth, and they will last a thousand years.
Your fortune is an iron enclosure;
Hero, your people are your countenance!
My son, become khan of a royal court,
A man of dignity,
Splitting a black hair with perfect judgment,
A soul endowed with sacred grace;
Become the giant called Khan Seytek!
My son, rule a blessed people!
If you seek land, here is the land of Talas;
Here is the mighty Kyrgyz nation.
My son, one who drinks when offered yet is never filled,
Whose greed never ceases,
Who, when driven through darkness,
Stalks like a tiger;
No mortal has dared confront him,
And no mortal facing him has prevailed.
This is the blessing I bestow
Upon my heroic Kyrgyz people.
If you receive them as your own father would,
Your road ahead will be white;
If you lead your countless host,
Be discerning when they stray;
Observe and value your inheritance.
Do not blurt out your innermost secrets,
For the greatest treasure and richest wealth is this:
My son, do not wound the people’s hearts!”
When he had given this blessing,
He was both their shelter and their mountain—
The heroic elder Bakai,
A saint offering his prayer.
Receiving the blessing of Khan Bakai,
The hero Seytek became a warrior,
A prince upheld by the spirits;
All twelve parts of his body reached perfection,
And he became a lion who maintained a court,
A man with multitudes behind him,
Khan over the whole universe.
He joined what had been severed,
And the nation thundered with joy.
Then Seytek’s
Forefather, old Bakai,
His dear grandmother Kanykey,
The sacred saint,
Semetey, son of Manas,
That dear lion upheld by the spirits,
The hero raised by fairies,
Who was found after twelve years—
Brave Semetey, the lionhearted warrior—
Was stricken at that very time
With an illness that left his ears unable to hear.
The moonlike lady Aichürök
Now sent word among the people.
Then they placed upon Seytek
A golden crown,
And seated him on the golden throne,
Making him a saintly sovereign,
And khan of the nation with its royal court.
Saying “Amen,” they made the gray-maned hero
A saintly sovereign,
And raised him up as khan!
Thus brave Seytek
Became the sultan.
He matured and became a warrior,
The equal of every valiant son,
A ruler of the people,
While all who opposed him were laid low—
Such was the youth he became.
There was no regret even in death,
And no one remained to turn back the herding crook.
The two reins and the single lead-rope
Were willingly placed in his hands.
At the very outset his heart
Bloomed like a flower and found peace;
The gray-maned Seytek became khan.
The people lived serenely, the nation rejoiced,
And the dear people regained their splendor.
No darkness remained; the lamp shone,
And the dear people came into the sunlight.
The hero Seytek became khan,
And every enemy who challenged him was laid low;
The fearsome foe was defeated,
And upon the dear people, like peaceful waters,
The days of happiness were showered.
He became khan and maintained a court,
A man of dignity;
Riding proudly, he governed the people,
Splitting a black hair with perfect judgment—
Brave Seytek was just.
His army numbered six vast divisions,
And he became khan of a mighty nation;
Thus did Seytek live.
Let us leave this tale here
And begin the news
Of Kuyaly of Kayypchal.
Maiden Kuyaly, the lionhearted champion,
Spoke softly but struck firm,
And began to speak in the court
To the gray-maned hero Semetey:
“When we depart for Judgment Day,
You will be the companion who comforts my soul.
For the guilt bringing hell upon the maiden,
When the hour came to grapple,
I invoked the name of God;
I made a binding vow.
I crushed the one who caused grief,
And checked your enemy;
Your foe Sarybay—
I killed him and burned his bones.
I measured out his life and brought it back.
I shouted in fury
And scattered his ashes into the sky.
Now that I have seen the one I watched for,
Now that my wish has been granted,
As yesterday we chewed white wheaten flour together
And wrestled after reciting the creed,
Remain true to that solemn oath!
Give me your pledged hand.
You are the support around which I gird my belt,
And on my appointed Resurrection Day
You are the husband I choose to wed—
Such is my desire.
This is the hour for which I have watched;
On the soiled road toward Judgment Day,
You are the companion who will clasp my hand.
My hero of boundless treasure,
Having battled with Alma,
You became Ur’s son.
I, being Ur's daughter,
We shall plunge into merriment,
If the words spoken are true.
Sharing meat from one cauldron,
Sharing one delight,
Easing our aching longing,
Walking arm in arm,
We shall lie in each other's embrace.
In great delight and merriment
We shall immerse ourselves in joy.
Our destination is Jelpiniş;
Wearying horses, ranging the land,
Unleashing hounds and flying birds,
Binding tassels to our steel spears,
And farther on, warring with foes,
Sarybai is the one I will drive off—
Such is the foe I shall grapple with…
The Creator restored my senses,
And brought me to you, gray-maned wolf;
We lodged together as guests,
And shared the name of warrior.
In this mortal world
We steeped ourselves in pleasure,
And lay upon one bed.
Our bodies entwined, our blood mingled,
We turned to each other and joined our souls.
My noble one, born for me,
My companion until Judgment Day,
My heart yearns for my people,
For the people called wretched.
My people once found gold,
Yet spirits would ravage them.
What has become of my dear homeland?
Without broad expanses there is no land;
No man is brave who misses not his people,
And there must be no fewer than fifty men.
Why should I crave too deeply
The pleasures of this two-day world?
Let me reach my dear people.
Forgive my unfulfilled longing,
And relinquish your claim upon me,”—
So Kuyaly spoke,
Biting her finger and shaking her head;
They clasped hands in farewell,
Making the face of the earth resound,
And galloped toward Jelpiniş.
She found what she desired
And encountered the bloodthirsty hero;
Kuyaly of Kaiypchal
Now set out upon the champion’s road.
Semetey led the five doomed heroes—
“Our journey has grown long;
The time to die has come,
And this world has grown narrow.
Why should we remain any longer?
Let us enter a place
Unknown to man or nation,”—
Said Bakai and Kanykei,
